apmo-1997-01.title: Telescoping, then the harmonic series
apmo-1997-01.body:
**The denominators.** The $n$-th triangular number is $t_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, so
$$\frac1{t_1}+\dots+\frac1{t_n}=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{2}{k(k+1)}=2\sum_{k=1}^n\left(\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}\right)=\frac{2n}{n+1}.$$
The last denominator ends with $\frac1{1993006}$ and $1993006=\frac{1996\cdot1997}2=t_{1996}$. So the terms of $S$ are $\frac{n+1}{2n}$ for $n=1,\dots,1996$ (the first one is $\frac22=1$), and
$$S=\sum_{n=1}^{1996}\frac{n+1}{2n}=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{1996}\left(1+\frac1n\right)=\frac12\left(1996+H_{1996}\right),\qquad H_m=1+\frac12+\dots+\frac1m .$$

**$H_{1996}>6$.** For $j\ge1$, the block $\frac1{2^{j-1}+1}+\dots+\frac1{2^j}$ has $2^{j-1}$ terms, each $\ge\frac1{2^j}$, so it is $\ge\frac12$. Hence
$$H_{2^{10}}=1+\sum_{j=1}^{10}\left(\frac1{2^{j-1}+1}+\dots+\frac1{2^j}\right)\ge1+\frac{10}2=6,$$
and since $2^{10}=1024<1996$, $H_{1996}>H_{1024}\ge6$.

Therefore $S>\frac12(1996+6)=1001$. ∎

apmo-1997-02.title: Look for $n=2pq$
apmo-1997-02.body:
**Why $n=2\cdot$odd.** Since $2^n+2=2(2^{n-1}+1)$ and $2^{n-1}+1$ is odd, $n$ must be $2r$ with $r$ odd, and we need $r\mid 2^{n-1}+1$. For a prime $p\mid r$ this says $2^{n-1}\equiv-1\pmod p$, so the order of $2$ modulo $p$ divides $2(n-1)$ but not $n-1$. Searching among $n=2pq$ with small primes (the official solution does this systematically, using $p-1\mid 4pq-2$ from Fermat's little theorem) leads to $p=11$, $q=43$, $n=946$. (The same idea gives $n=66=2\cdot3\cdot11$, which is too small.)

**Check that $n=946$ works.** $946=2\cdot11\cdot43$ and $2^{946}+2=2(2^{945}+1)$, so it suffices to show $11\mid2^{945}+1$ and $43\mid 2^{945}+1$.
- Modulo $11$: $2^5=32\equiv-1$, so $2^{10}\equiv1$. Since $945=94\cdot10+5$, $2^{945}\equiv2^5\equiv-1\pmod{11}$.
- Modulo $43$: $2^7=128=3\cdot43-1\equiv-1$, so $2^{14}\equiv1$. Since $945=67\cdot14+7$, $2^{945}\equiv2^7\equiv-1\pmod{43}$.

Hence $473=11\cdot43$ divides $2^{945}+1$, and $946=2\cdot473$ divides $2(2^{945}+1)=2^{946}+2$. (In fact $946$ is the only such $n$ in the range.)

**Answer: 946**

apmo-1997-03.title: Compute $l_a$, then AM-GM and Euler
apmo-1997-03.body:
Use the usual notation $a,b,c$ for the sides, $R$ and $r$ for the circumradius and inradius. Let the bisector from $A$ meet $BC$ at $L$ and the circle again at $K$, so $m_a=AL$, $M_a=AK$.

**$m_aM_a=bc$.** Triangles $ABL$ and $AKC$ are similar: $\angle BAL=\angle KAC$ (bisector) and $\angle ABL=\angle ABC=\angle AKC$ (inscribed angles on arc $AC$). Hence $\frac{AB}{AK}=\frac{AL}{AC}$, i.e. $AL\cdot AK=bc$.

**$m_a^2$.** By the intersecting chords theorem $AL\cdot LK=BL\cdot LC$, and by the angle bisector theorem $BL=\frac{ac}{b+c}$, $LC=\frac{ab}{b+c}$. So
$$m_a^2=AL\cdot AK-AL\cdot LK=bc-\frac{a^2bc}{(b+c)^2}.$$

**$l_a$.** Therefore $l_a=\dfrac{m_a}{M_a}=\dfrac{m_a^2}{m_aM_a}=1-\dfrac{a^2}{(b+c)^2}$, and with $\sin A=\frac a{2R}$:
$$\frac{l_a}{\sin^2A}=4R^2\left(\frac1{a^2}-\frac1{(b+c)^2}\right),$$
and similarly for $b$ and $c$.

**Estimate.** Since $(b+c)^2\ge4bc$, $\frac1{(b+c)^2}\le\frac1{4bc}$; and $\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\ge\frac1{ab}+\frac1{bc}+\frac1{ca}$ (this is $x^2+y^2+z^2\ge xy+yz+zx$). So
$$\sum\frac{l_a}{\sin^2A}\ge4R^2\left(\sum\frac1{a^2}-\frac14\sum\frac1{bc}\right)\ge4R^2\cdot\frac34\sum\frac1{bc}=3R^2\,\frac{a+b+c}{abc}.$$
Now $abc=4R\cdot[ABC]$ and $[ABC]=r\cdot\frac{a+b+c}2$, so
$$3R^2\,\frac{a+b+c}{abc}=\frac{3R^2(a+b+c)}{2Rr(a+b+c)}=\frac{3R}{2r}\ge3$$
by Euler's inequality $R\ge2r$ (from $OI^2=R(R-2r)$).

**Equality.** Equality in $(b+c)^2\ge4bc$ (and its analogues) requires $b=c$, $c=a$, $a=b$, so the triangle is equilateral. Conversely, if $ABC$ is equilateral then $l_a=1-\frac14=\frac34=\sin^2A$, so each term is $1$ and the sum is $3$. ∎

apmo-1997-04.title: A spiral similarity
apmo-1997-04.body:
Write $T_n$ for the closed triangle $A_{n-2}A_{n-1}A_n$ ($n\ge3$).

**Shape of the sequence.** By induction, $T_n$ has a right angle at $A_n$. This holds for $n=3$; if $T_n$ is right-angled at $A_n$, then $A_{n+1}$ is the foot of the altitude from the right angle, so it lies strictly inside the hypotenuse $A_{n-2}A_{n-1}$, and $T_{n+1}=A_{n-1}A_nA_{n+1}$ has a right angle at $A_{n+1}$. In particular $T_{n+1}\subset T_n$ for all $n$.

**Coordinates.** Use complex numbers with $A_3=0$, $A_1=i$ (unit $=A_1A_3$) and $A_2=s$, $s$ real, $s\ne0$. The line $A_1A_2$ is $\frac xs+y=1$, the foot of the perpendicular from $0$ is $A_4=\frac{s+is^2}{1+s^2}$, and the foot from $A_4$ to the real axis $A_2A_3$ is $A_5=\frac{s}{1+s^2}$. Put
$$\mu=\frac{s}{1+s^2},\qquad \lambda=i\mu,\qquad S(z)=\lambda z+\mu .$$
Then $S(A_1)=-\mu+\mu=0=A_3$, $S(A_2)=\mu(1+is)=A_4$, $S(A_3)=\mu=A_5$. $S$ is a rotation by $\pm90^\circ$ combined with a scaling by $|\lambda|=\frac{|s|}{1+s^2}\le\frac12$.

**$S(A_k)=A_{k+2}$ for all $k$.** True for $k=1,2,3$. A similarity maps the foot of a perpendicular from a point to a line onto the foot of the perpendicular from the image point to the image line. If it holds up to $k$ ($k\ge3$), then $A_{k+1}$ is the foot from $A_k$ to $A_{k-2}A_{k-1}$, so $S(A_{k+1})$ is the foot from $A_{k+2}$ to $A_kA_{k+1}$, which is $A_{k+3}$.

**(a)** Hence $T_{n+2}=S(T_n)$ and $\operatorname{diam}T_{n+2}\le\frac12\operatorname{diam}T_n\to0$. The $T_n$ are nested non-empty compact sets with diameters tending to $0$, so their intersection is a single point $P$. Since $S$ is a bijection, $S\bigl(\bigcap_n T_n\bigr)=\bigcap_n T_{n+2}=\bigcap_nT_n$, so $S(P)=P$.

$P$ is not one of the points $A_m$: if $P=A_m$ ($m\ge2$), then $A_{m+2}=S(A_m)=S(P)=P=A_m$, but $A_{m+2}$ lies strictly inside segment $A_{m-1}A_m$; and $P=A_1$ would give $A_3=S(A_1)=A_1$.

$P$ is interior to every $T_n$: $A_{n+1}$ and $A_{n+2}$ lie strictly inside two different sides of $T_n$ (namely $A_{n-2}A_{n-1}$ and $A_{n-1}A_n$), and $A_{n+3}$ lies strictly inside segment $A_nA_{n+1}$, a cevian of $T_n$, hence in the interior of $T_n$. So every point of $T_{n+3}=A_{n+1}A_{n+2}A_{n+3}$ other than $A_{n+1},A_{n+2}$ is interior to $T_n$. As $P\in T_{n+3}$ and $P\ne A_{n+1},A_{n+2}$, $P$ is interior to $T_n$. Any point interior to all $T_n$ lies in $\bigcap T_n=\{P\}$, so $P$ is the only one. $\square$

**(b)** Now $A_1,A_3$ are fixed and $A_2$ is any point $\ne A_3$ of the line through $A_3$ perpendicular to $A_1A_3$, i.e. $s$ runs over all non-zero reals. From $S(P)=P$ and $S(A_1)=A_3$ we get $A_3-P=\lambda(A_1-P)$. Since $\lambda$ is purely imaginary, $PA_3\perp PA_1$, so $P$ lies on the circle $\Gamma$ with diameter $A_1A_3$, and
$$\tan\angle PA_1A_3=\frac{PA_3}{PA_1}=|\lambda|=\frac{|s|}{1+s^2}.$$
Also $P=\frac{\mu}{1-i\mu}=\frac{\mu(1+i\mu)}{1+\mu^2}$ has real part of the sign of $s$: $P$ is on the same side of line $A_1A_3$ as $A_2$.

As $s$ runs over $(0,\infty)$, $\frac{s}{1+s^2}$ takes every value in $(0,\frac12]$ (it tends to $0$ as $s\to0$ and equals $\frac12$ at $s=1$), and the same for $s<0$ on the other side. Since $A_1A_3$ is a diameter of length $1$, $PA_3=\sin\angle PA_1A_3$, and $\tan\theta\le\frac12\iff\sin\theta\le\frac1{\sqrt5}$ for acute $\theta$.

**Answer (b):** the locus is the set of points $P$ on the circle with diameter $A_1A_3$ with $0<PA_3\le\frac{A_1A_3}{\sqrt5}$: two arcs symmetric about $A_1A_3$, starting at $A_3$ (excluded) and ending at the points obtained for $A_3A_2=A_3A_1$ (included; with $A_3=(0,0)$, $A_1=(0,1)$ these are $(\pm\frac25,\frac15)$). ∎

apmo-1997-05.title: Reduce to a median problem
apmo-1997-05.body:
**Setting up.** Let $x_i$ be the net number of objects passed from $A_i$ to $A_{i+1}$ (negative if objects go from $A_{i+1}$ to $A_i$), with $x_0=x_n$. Across the edge $A_iA_{i+1}$ at least $|x_i|$ objects must be moved, so the total transferred is at least $\sum|x_i|$; we will see this is attained.

At the end $A_i$ has $a_i-x_i+x_{i-1}=N$. For $i=2,\dots,n$ this gives $x_i=x_{i-1}+a_i-N$, so
$$x_i=x_1-\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha_i=(i-1)N-(a_2+a_3+\dots+a_i),\quad \alpha_1=0 .$$
The remaining equation (for $i=1$) is then automatic because $\sum a_i=nN$. So the possible redistributions are given by the free integer $x_1$, and we must minimise
$$F(x_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n|x_1-\alpha_i| .$$

**Median.** Sort the $\alpha_i$ as $\beta_1\le\beta_2\le\dots\le\beta_n$. For each $j\le n/2$, $|x-\beta_j|+|x-\beta_{n+1-j}|\ge\beta_{n+1-j}-\beta_j$, with equality iff $\beta_j\le x\le\beta_{n+1-j}$. Adding these (and the term $|x-\beta_{(n+1)/2}|\ge0$ when $n$ is odd), $F(x)\ge\sum_{j\le n/2}(\beta_{n+1-j}-\beta_j)$, with equality exactly when $x$ is a median: $x=\beta_{(n+1)/2}$ for odd $n$, and $\beta_{n/2}\le x\le\beta_{n/2+1}$ for even $n$. Take $x_1=\beta_{\lceil n/2\rceil}$ (an integer).

**The transfers can be carried out.** With this choice $x_1=\alpha_k$ for some $k$, so $x_k=0$: nothing crosses the edge $A_kA_{k+1}$, and the transfers live on a path. Orient each edge in the direction of its transfer; a path has no directed cycles, so we can order the people so that everybody acts after all neighbours who send to them. When $A_i$ acts, they have received everything due to them and hold $a_i+(\text{received})=N+(\text{to send})\ge(\text{to send})$ objects, so they can send their amounts. Each edge then carries exactly $|x_i|$ objects.

**Answer:** pass $x_i=x_1-\alpha_i$ objects from $A_i$ to $A_{i+1}$ (from $A_{i+1}$ to $A_i$ if negative), where $\alpha_i=(i-1)N-\sum_{j=2}^i a_j$ and $x_1$ is a median of $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$; the minimum total is $\sum_i|x_1-\alpha_i|$. ∎
